proposed_edges.relationship: Smout’s ‘The Highlands and the Roots of Green Consciousness’ (1991; lecture 1990) invokes Keith Thomas’s Man and the Natural World (1983) for the eighteenth-century change in educated attitudes to nature.
proposed_edges.map_label: Thomas on changing attitudes to nature
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh OCR reading of the official British Academy scan, printed pp. 238–239 and n. 8. Smout explicitly credits ‘Keith Thomas in particular’ for describing this change; n. 8 identifies the 1983 book. The surrounding argument distinguishes earlier Scottish appreciation of nature from the later changes among educated outsiders. This is a named intellectual resource, not a claim that Thomas originated Scottish environmental awareness. Thomas’s book itself unread; the lecture was delivered in 1990 and published in 1991.

proposed_edges.relationship: Keith Thomas's review 'The Long March' (1984) cites Smout's 'Scotland and England' (1980) for the point that primary-producing regions such as Scotland broke out of the trap and industrialized, as part of the 'sharp attack' on the core–periphery world-economy argument developed by Wallerstein.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Thomas’s 1984 review, passage beginning ‘Even more debatable’ through the paragraph beginning ‘In recent years’, plus n. 7. He names Wallerstein, explains the core–periphery claim, then cites Smout for primary producers escaping the industrialization trap. Smout’s Review 3:4 (1980), pp. 601–630, is unread; those pages are citation metadata, not pages consulted. Thomas reviews Braudel and distinguishes the two theorists. No wholesale rejection of world-systems analysis or account of Wallerstein’s reply is proposed. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Thomas's 'Even more debatable' paragraph names Wallerstein's world-economy concept; 'In recent years ... Scotland, Denmark, Australia are obvious examples.' carries n. 7 citing Smout, 'Scotland and England: Is Dependency a Symptom or a Cause of Underdevelopment?', Review iii.4 (1980). Support is a single footnote attached to a sentence that also lists Denmark and Australia, and the 'kind of argument' attacked is the Braudel/Wallerstein world-economy thesis just quoted from Braudel. Edge is acceptable only as an explicitly mediated, footnote-level attribution; the current sentence slightly overstates by saying Thomas 'reads' Smout's article.]

proposed_edges.relationship: Smout’s ‘Land and Sea: The Environment’ (2012) cites McNeill’s Something New Under the Sun (2000) for Glasgow’s coal-smoke pollution and its burden on human health.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authorized preview, printed p. 29, first paragraph and n. 29, freshly read. Smout quotes ‘experienced newspaper editors left extra space for obituaries during smog sieges’ and gives Glasgow mortality and soot figures; n. 29 explicitly cites McNeill (2000), pp. 63, 66, 70–71. Those are Smout’s references, not pages independently read here. McNeill’s book and quantitative estimates remain unverified. A specific evidential use, not adoption of McNeill’s entire framework.
